title: What Does Learning Look like in Action - 3
author: Martin Skelton
summary: This instalment of Skelton's learning-states series describes the second state, consolidating learning, using childhood car journeys, learning the saxophone and learning to drive as analogies. He explains that the brain begins to hardwire repeated experiences, and that teachers can see this in students who need help less often, correct their own work and show growing confidence. He stresses that judging the shift from new to consolidating learning is a professional judgement call, not a precise measurement. The state brings good news in rising motivation and bad news in overconfidence, which tempts teachers, parents and coaches to move learners on too early. Moving too slowly is also costly, breeding boredom and wasting time, so he urges close attention to evidence about each learner.
points: Consolidating learning looks like reduced need for help, self-correction and growing confidence, though the boundary with new learning is a judgement call.
The brain hardwires experiences that repeat often enough, which is why practice makes routine tasks like driving automatic.
Consolidation feels rewarding and builds motivation, but that confidence can trick learners and adults into thinking learning is stickier than it is.
Moving learners on too soon produces shallow learning of many things, while moving too slowly breeds boredom and wastes time.
quotes: Looking for what is happening during ‘New Learning’ as we see it in front of us is both imprecise and super helpful. It is a judgement call. We are rarely going to be exactly ‘right’.

Our brains begin to ‘recognise’ that the repeated experiences they are having are frequent enough to warrant saving energy through some hardwiring. And later, as these experiences continue to happen, the brain starts to speed the process up as the neuronal connections become more secure.

A few months later, with good support and plenty of repeated experiences, we drive the same stretch of road with more ease. Some things are already more automatic by now, if not completely so. We have time to turn on the car radio while driving, take a quick glance at a child in the back seat or think about the shopping we are about to do, whilst our brain takes care of all those things that just a relatively short while earlier seemed, frankly, impossible.

In my many visits to work with teachers and students in classrooms the first thing I look for is good struggling; students who are willing to stumble the early rocky path of learning and keep going, making mistakes, taking frequent advice, repeating their experiences frequently, occasionally losing heart but usually getting themselves back in the game. Usually, this is a very good sign for me.

Sometimes, though, these good feelings breed over-confidence or poor judgement. This over-confidence causes us to think that things are stickier than they are, to stop our current repeated experiences and move on to more new learning before we are really ready for it, before our current learning has become genuinely hard-wired.

Often, this is where teachers, parents and coaches make their biggest mistake by moving the learner on too soon. Moving on to the next chunk of new learning before the previous chunk has experienced an appropriately long consolidating stage just means that we end up ‘learning’ lots of stuff not very well.
On the other hand, moving too slowly through the consolidating stage can help us learn to be demotivated, to learn to be bored. It also wastes learning time.
